title: Pick the agent's home
brief: An agent needs somewhere to run. How much code you own, where that code may run and whether each user needs private files and compute are all open. Compare five homes and flip the dials.

blocks.md:
Foundry Agent Service has three agent types [[r1]]. A **prompt agent** is instructions, a model and tools as configuration, with no code. A **voice-based prompt agent** adds managed real-time voice over a WebSocket and is preview as of 2026-10-13. A **hosted agent** runs your own code as a container image, or as a .zip that Foundry builds into an image [[r2]].

You can also skip the agent resource. Call the Responses API directly and the definition lives in your code: an *ephemeral agent*. Two homes sit outside the service, self-hosting on AKS or Container Apps and Copilot Studio, and both can still be governed (level 6). Treat the choice as a dial problem, not a ranking.

All of it sits in one resource model: a Foundry resource (`Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts` with kind `AIServices`) holds projects, and a project is the development boundary. Connected Storage, Key Vault and AI Search keep their own governance [[r24]].

options.name: Prompt agent
options.summary: Instructions, model and tools as configuration. No code and no container.
pros: Least to manage, per the agent types page
No container to build or size
cons: No custom orchestration or protocol surface
options.bestWhen: Instructions, a model and catalog tools are enough.
options.avoidWhen: You need webhooks, AG-UI, voice sockets or files that persist across turns.

options.name: Hosted agent
options.summary: Your code in a per-session, VM-isolated sandbox with its own Entra agent identity and endpoint.
pros: Python or C# with Agent Framework, LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK, Anthropic Agent SDK, GitHub Copilot SDK or custom code
cons: Billing follows active sessions, so concurrency times allocation drives cost
Some hosted features are still preview on 2026-10-13, such as long-running resilience
The initial-preview backend ended on 2026-08-20 and forced a redeploy
options.bestWhen: You bring code, custom protocols or per-session state.
options.avoidWhen: A prompt agent already covers the need, or the code must run outside Azure.

meta.v: CPU and memory of active sessions

options.name: Direct Responses call (ephemeral agent)
options.summary: Your app calls the Responses API. The definition ships with the app and no Foundry agent resource exists.
pros: Definition versions with your app code
cons: Nothing for Foundry to version, publish or give an endpoint to
You own the loop, hosting and scaling
options.bestWhen: The agent is a feature of one application.
options.avoidWhen: Several teams must share, version and publish the agent as a unit.

options.name: Self-host on AKS or Container Apps
options.summary: Run the agent on your own platform, on another cloud or on premises, then register it for governance.
pros: Code and data can stay on another cloud or on premises
Registry sync, the Agent 365 SDK or Foundry Control Plane registration can still govern it
cons: You run scaling, isolation, patching and identity wiring
Native integration paths give more than inventory; registration alone may not
options.bestWhen: Residency or an existing platform forces the location.
options.avoidWhen: No hard reason exists to leave Foundry.

options.name: Copilot Studio agent
options.summary: A maker-oriented platform. Its agents appear in the Agent 365 registry and can receive agent identities (preview).
pros: Makers build without a code pipeline
Visible in the registry, sometimes under more than one type by design
cons: Less control over orchestration and protocols than owned code (inference)
Automatic agent identity assignment is preview as of 2026-10-13
options.bestWhen: Business teams own the agent and the tools are connector shaped.
options.avoidWhen: You need custom protocols or sandboxed code execution.

blocks.title: Pick a runtime
blocks.prompt: Flip the constraints. The ranking and the reasons update.

cfg.why: No code or container, the least to manage.

low.why: Configuration, but not a maker surface.

foundry.why: Managed in the service, private networking supported.

cfg.why: Compute billed per active session is wasted.

none.why: Works, but the sandbox adds cost.

foundry.why: Own endpoint, identity and BYO VNet.

away.why: The sandbox runs in Foundry, not on premises.

cfg.why: Works, but you host the loop.

code.why: You own orchestration inside the app.

low.why: It is code in an app.

foundry.why: Fine, the app lives in your estate.

away.why: Only model calls leave your environment.

foundry.why: You rebuild what the service gives you.

away.why: Code stays where it must, then you register it.

foundry.why: Runs in the Microsoft platform and shows in the registry.

away.why: Not a place for on-premises code.

blocks.takeaway: Hosted agents win on code plus state, prompt agents win on least effort, self-hosting wins on location. Name the dial that decided it.

blocks.title: Runtime decision path
blocks.alt: A decision tree: custom code needed leads to a hosted agent when it can run in Foundry or self-hosting when it cannot. No custom code leads to a prompt agent.

blocks.caption: Governance is a separate decision from the runtime. All three paths can reach the control plane.

items.symptom: The bill grows with concurrency on a light agent
items.cause: A hosted agent sized above its need, billed on CPU and memory of every active session
items.fix: Use a prompt agent if no code is needed, or move to a smaller sandbox. Detect it by watching peak CPU against allocation.

items.symptom: The portal cannot publish the agent to Teams
items.cause: Portal publishing is not supported when the project has public network access disabled
items.fix: Publish through the REST API with `enable_m365_public_endpoint`.

items.symptom: Role assignments from an older runbook do not match the portal
items.cause: Azure AI User, Azure AI Owner, Azure AI Account Owner and Azure AI Project Manager were renamed Foundry User, Foundry Owner, Foundry Account Owner and Foundry Project Manager
items.fix: The role IDs did not change. Update the runbook names [[r24]].

blocks.title: What interviewers listen for
blocks.md: Do not say 'hosted agents for everything'. Name what forces code, then name the cost: per-session compute and a preview boundary you checked on a date.

quiz.q: Requirements change: each user session needs files that persist across turns, a custom Invocations endpoint and compute isolated per session. Which home fits best?
options: Direct Responses call from a stateless web app
quiz.explain: Hosted agents give a per-session VM-isolated sandbox, a persisted `$HOME` and several protocols. A prompt agent has no code or sandbox. Copilot Studio is a maker platform without per-session sandboxes. A stateless app would have to build file persistence and isolation itself.

quiz.q: A team cannot publish a hosted agent to Teams from the Foundry portal. Which cause fits the project setting shown?

code.code:
project.publicNetworkAccess = Disabled
portal publish -> not supported

options: The agent exposes no A2A endpoint, which Teams requires before any publishing can start in the portal
The Azure Bot Service provider is registered twice in the subscription
Portal publishing is unsupported with public network access disabled, so use the REST API route
Prompt agents and hosted agents cannot share one project
quiz.explain: The publish guide states portal publishing is unsupported when public network access is disabled and points to the REST API with `enable_m365_public_endpoint`. Teams does not need A2A, since the Activity protocol is bridged from Responses. A double provider registration is not a documented cause. Projects can hold both agent types.

quiz.q: Select every statement that holds on 2026-10-13.
options: A prompt agent needs no container image.
A direct Responses API call creates a Foundry agent resource you can publish.
A hosted agent can be built from a container image or from a .zip.
The Foundry GA table lists hosted agents on their own GA row.
quiz.explain: Prompt agents are configuration only, and hosted agents accept a container image or a .zip that Foundry builds. A direct Responses call is an ephemeral agent with no agent resource, so there is nothing to publish. The migration page states hosted agents are generally available on the GA v1 API (azure-ai-projects 2.3.0 or later), but the GA table has no separate hosted row, so the table row claim is not supported.

takeaways: Runtime is a dial problem: logic ownership, state and location
Hosted agents buy code and per-session state, and cost scales with active sessions
No separate hosted row exists in the GA table, though the migration page says hosted agents are GA on the v1 API
Governance is a separate decision from the runtime
